claim: The guanine-sensing riboswitch from Bacillus subtilis (GSW) negatively regulates the transcription of the xpt-gene by the premature termination of RNA synthesis.
source: The guanine-sensing riboswitch from Bacillus subtilis (GSW) negatively regulates the transcription of the xpt-gene by the premature termination of RNA synthesis (Mandal et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mandal et al., 2003

claim: The full-length guanine-sensing riboswitch adopts the terminator conformation irrespective of the presence or absence of ligand.
source: Regardless of the presence or absence of the cognate ligand, the RNA adopts a single conformation in which the terminator helix (TH) is formed as inferred from NMR signals (for assignment, see Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) arising from the stable GU base-pairs (U129-G147 and U130-G146) (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by NMR spectroscopy data showing stable GU base-pairs characteristic of the terminator helix

claim: The terminator conformation in the full-length construct is stabilized by at least ΔΔG > 8 kJ mol−1 compared to the antiterminator conformation.
source: Since the terminator conformation in the full-length construct is the only detectable state regardless of the presence or absence of ligand, it must be stabilised by at least △△G > 8 kJ mol−1 compared to the antiterminator conformation at a NMR signal-to-noise greater than 10:1.
evidence: Inferred from NMR detection limits and the absence of observable antiterminator signals

claim: Multiple transcription intermediates accumulate during synthesis of the full-length riboswitch.
source: In multiple round transcription reactions, we detected several distinct shorter RNA products (Figure 1e). Three of the detected fragments correspond to the aptamer domain (nucleotides 10–89), to the prematurely terminated form (nucleotides 10–164), and to the full-length of the mRNA-5'-UTR.
evidence: Supported by PAGE analysis showing distinct RNA fragments

claim: Two additional RNA fragments of 100 and 140 nucleotides represent canonical transcriptional pause sites.
source: Furthermore, two additional fragments of 100 and 140 nucleotides are detected. These latter RNAs exhibit 3'-terminal stretches of U-residues and therefore represent canonical transcriptional pause sites (Landick, 2006; Larson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by detection of U-rich sequences characteristic of pause sites and citations to literature on pause sites

claim: The truncated riboswitch GSWPAT populates two equally intense conformations GSW[PA]T and GSWP[AT] that differ in the formation of mutually exclusive helices PA or AT.
source: For GSWPAT, we observed two equally intense sets of NMR signals from two long-lived conformations GSW[PA]T and GSWP[AT] (Figure 1b,c) that differ with regard to the formation of the two mutually exclusive helices PA or AT.
evidence: Supported by NMR spectroscopy showing two sets of signals with equal intensity

claim: Addition of ligand to GSWPAT shifts the conformational equilibrium towards GSW[PA]T.
source: Upon addition of ligand, we detect ligand binding and subsequent shifting of the conformational equilibrium towards GSW[PA]T (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by NMR data showing changes in signal intensities upon ligand addition

claim: The antiterminator conformation is a thermodynamically stable state of the GSWPAT transcription intermediate in the absence of ligand.
source: Thus, in contrast to the full-length riboswitch, the antiterminator conformation representing the functional on-state is a thermodynamically stable state (GSWP[AT]) of this transcription intermediate (GSWPAT) in the absence of ligand.
evidence: Inferred from NMR data showing equal populations of both conformations

claim: Addition of equimolar amounts of Ttrans to GSWPA without ligand leads to formation of the antiterminator conformation mimic containing helix AT.
source: Without ligand, addition of equimolar amounts of Ttrans to GSWPA led to formation of the antiterminator conformation mimic containing helix AT and the strand P is unpaired (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by isotope-filter NMR experiments showing formation of AT helix

claim: The GSWPA-Ttrans complex is disrupted by the addition of ligand.
source: This GSWPA-Ttrans complex was disrupted by the addition of ligand (Figure 2d), restoring formation of helix PA.
evidence: Supported by NMR data showing dissociation of AT helix and reformation of PA helix upon ligand addition

claim: The presence of ligand stabilizes GSWPA so that subsequent addition of Ttrans does not disrupt helix PA.
source: In contrast, the presence of ligand stabilised GSWPA so that subsequent addition of Ttrans did not disrupt helix PA in the aptamer domain within the GSWPA-ligand-complex and formation of the antiterminator helix was suppressed.
evidence: Supported by NMR experiments showing PA helix remains intact when ligand is present before Ttrans addition

claim: Ligand binding to GSWPA represents the structural decision point.
source: From these findings, we can conclude that ligand binding to GSWPA represents the structural decision point.
evidence: Inferred from NMR experiments showing that ligand binding determines whether AT or PA helix forms

claim: Addition of Htrans to the antiterminator conformation induces a conformational switch characterized by formation of the terminator helix TH and helix PA, regardless of ligand presence.
source: Regardless of the presence or the absence of ligand, addition of Htrans to the antiterminator conformation in the GSWPA-Ttrans complex induced a conformational switch characterized by the formation of the terminator helix TH and the helix PA (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: Supported by NMR experiments showing formation of TH upon Htrans addition

claim: Ligand binding to GSWPA is fast with a rate constant k1 of (2.4 ± 0.3) × 10−1 s−1.
source: Indeed, ligand binding to GSWPA either in the absence or in presence of the terminator helix (Figure 3f and g) was fast, with a k1 of (2.4 ± 0.3) 10−1 s−1, and induced a slower tertiary structure rearrangement (k2 = [1.8 ± 0.2) 10−2 s−1] within the aptamer, consistent with previous experiments (Vogel and Jensen, 1994; Reeder and Hawley, 1996).
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements

claim: Ligand binding to GSWPA induces a slower tertiary structure rearrangement with k2 = (1.8 ± 0.2) × 10−2 s−1.
source: Indeed, ligand binding to GSWPA either in the absence or in presence of the terminator helix (Figure 3f and g) was fast, with a k1 of (2.4 ± 0.3) 10−1 s−1, and induced a slower tertiary structure rearrangement (k2 = [1.8 ± 0.2) 10−2 s−1] within the aptamer, consistent with previous experiments (Vogel and Jensen, 1994; Reeder and Hawley, 1996).
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements

claim: Formation of the terminator helix from single strands is rapid with k1 = (1.4 ± 0.8) × 10−1 s−1.
source: Subsequent formation of the terminator helix from single strands was also rapid (k1 = [1.4 ± 0.8] 10−1 s−1; Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements

claim: In the absence of ligand, GSWPA and Ttrans anneal rapidly to form the antiterminator complex with k = (9 ± 5) × 10−3 s−1.
source: In the absence of ligand, GSWPA and Ttrans anneal rapidly to form the antiterminator complex (k = [9 ± 5] 10−3 s−1; Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements

claim: The dissociation of the antiterminator helix AT is rate-limiting and slow with k1 = (0.5 ± 0.2) × 10−3 s−1.
source: Under these conditions, the dissociation of the antiterminator helix AT was rate-limiting and slow (k1 = [0.5 ± 0.2] 10−3 s−1; k2 = (1.1 ± 0.4) 10−4 s−1[Ttrans intrinsic unfolding, Figure 3—figure supplement 1]).
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements when Htrans is added to GSWPA-Ttrans complex

claim: The dissociation of helix AT is accelerated by the presence of ligand with k = (0.89 ± 0.09) × 10−3 s−1.
source: Importantly, the dissociation of helix P4 was accelerated by the presence of ligand, but in a concentration-independent manner above equimolar ratios (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; k = [0.89 ± 0.09] 10−3 s−1; Figure 2d)
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements at different ligand concentrations

claim: The AT conformation represents a meta-stable state that slowly refolds into the thermodynamically stable terminator state.
source: From these kinetic data (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3i), we conclude that the AT conformation represents a meta-stable state that slowly refolds into the thermodynamically stable terminator state (which represents the state of lowest free energy).
evidence: Inferred from kinetic data showing slow dissociation of AT helix

claim: The dissociation of PA is slow compared to the polymerase transcription speed.
source: The dissociation of PA is slow compared to the polymerase transcription speed.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of measured kinetic rates with transcription rates

claim: Transcriptional resting states are required to slow transcription to ensure sufficient time for the refolding of conformations [PA]T to P[AT] to enable riboswitch function.
source: Therefore, during mRNA synthesis, transcriptional resting states are required to slow transcription to ensure sufficient time for the refolding of conformations [PA]T to P[AT] to enable riboswitch function.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of refolding kinetics with transcription rates

claim: Transcription rates between 12 to 90 nucleotides per second have been reported in prokaryotes.
source: Transcription rates between 12 to 90 nucleotides per second have been reported in prokaryotes (Adelman et al., 2002; Vogel and Jensen, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on transcription rates

claim: A U6-stretch (U107-U112) is located between the aptamer domain and the terminator helix (pause site 1, PS1).
source: Within the sequence of GSW, a U6-stretch (U107-U112) is suspiciously located between the aptamer domain and the terminator helix (pause site 1, PS1) and between the A and T stretches of the antiterminator (U135-U141, pause site 2, PS2)
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of the riboswitch

claim: A U-stretch (U135-U141) is located between the A and T stretches of the antiterminator (pause site 2, PS2).
source: Within the sequence of GSW, a U6-stretch (U107-U112) is suspiciously located between the aptamer domain and the terminator helix (pause site 1, PS1) and between the A and T stretches of the antiterminator (U135-U141, pause site 2, PS2)
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of the riboswitch

claim: Seven transcribed RNAs could be identified in time-resolved single-round transcription assays.
source: Seven transcribed RNAs could be identified, suggesting that the formation of the shorter products after transcription of the aptamer domain and PS1 accumulate at a later time point during the overnight multi-round transcription.
evidence: Supported by PAGE analysis of transcription products

claim: The riboswitch maintains its ligand-response function during in vitro transcription assays, with termination efficiency increased by 24.8% for EcRNAP and by 30.3% for BsRNAP upon ligand addition.
source: The data indicate that the riboswitch maintains its ligand-response function during the in vitro transcription assays, as the termination efficiency is increased by 24.8% for EcRNAP and by 30.3% for BsRNAP.
evidence: Supported by quantification of terminated versus full-length transcripts in presence and absence of ligand

claim: Both E. coli and B. subtilis RNAPs pause longer at PS1 than at PS2.
source: Furthermore, the intensity of PS1 is stronger for BsRNAP transcription, indicating that PS1 has a higher influence on the elongation complex for the BsRNAP. In addition, the determined pausing-parameters (Supplementary file 1) show that both RNAPs pause longer at PS1 than at PS2.
evidence: Supported by analysis of pausing parameters from transcription assays

claim: The apparent transcription rates range from 0.4 ± 0.1 nt s−1 to 47.0 ± 53.3 nt s−1 for different transcription intermediates at 37°C.
source: The apparent transcription rates were determined to range from 0.4 ± 0.1 nt s−1 and 2.0 ± 0.5 nt s−1 (FL and GSWPATH) to 1.3 ± 0.6 nt s−1 and 47.0 ± 53.3 nt s−1 for the synthesis of the shorter transcription intermediates at 37°C (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved transcription assays

claim: Upon ligand addition, the apparent transcription rate decreased by at least a factor of two for PS2 and PS1.
source: Upon ligand addition, the apparent transcription rate decreased by at least a factor of two for PS2 and PS1 but was nearly identical for RNA95/RNA90 and RNA77.
evidence: Supported by comparison of transcription rates with and without ligand

claim: Multiple pausing events during transcription drastically decrease the apparent transcription rates of the longer RNAs FL and GSWPATH.
source: However, the multiple pausing events during transcription drastically decrease the apparent transcription rates of the longer RNAs FL and GSWPATH.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of transcription rates for different length transcripts

claim: Without pausing of the transcription machinery, riboswitch synthesis is fast compared to its own refolding reactions and the GSW does not reach a substantial population of conformations with the formed terminator.
source: Without pausing of the transcription machinery, riboswitch synthesis is fast compared to its own refolding reactions from apo- to holo-conformations. Therefore, the GSW does not reach a substantial population of conformations with the formed terminator [TH] and the polymerase escapes termination (Figure 5f,g).
evidence: Supported by kinetic Markov-model simulations using experimentally determined rates

claim: Pausing of transcription at pause site 1 opens a time window that allows for refolding of the riboswitch from the apo- to the holo-form.
source: In contrast, pausing of transcription at pause site 1 opens a time window that allows for refolding of the riboswitch from the apo- to the holo-form.
evidence: Supported by kinetic simulations showing increased off-state population with pausing

claim: A reduced rate of transcription after formation of the aptamer nucleotides due to pausing at PS1 results in higher population of off-states during synthesis before the polymerase leaves the point of decision.
source: Therefore, a reduced rate of transcription after formation of the aptamer nucleotides of the riboswitch due to pausing at PS1 in conjunction with a comparative slow conformational transition from [PA]T to P[AT] results in higher population of off-states during synthesis before the polymerase leaves the point of decision (Figure 5h,i).
evidence: Supported by kinetic simulations combining transcription and refolding rates

claim: Successive disruptive mutations (M1-M3) of PS1 correlate with the loss of regulation in vivo.
source: Successive disruptive mutations (M1-M3) of PS1 correlated with the loss of regulation in vivo (Figure 6a)
evidence: Supported by β-galactosidase reporter assays in B. subtilis

claim: Addition of further U residues to PS1 (M4) increased riboswitch efficiency.
source: and the addition of further U residues to PS1 (M4) increased riboswitch efficiency.
evidence: Supported by β-galactosidase reporter assays showing increased repression

claim: The loss of pause site integrity reduced the switching efficiency, whereas extended pausing of the RNA polymerase led to increased repression of reporter gene expression.
source: Monitoring the dose-dependence of the wild-type riboswitch compared to the M3 and M4 mutants indicated that the loss of pause site integrity reduced the switching efficiency, whereas extended pausing of the RNA polymerase led to increased repression of reporter gene expression (Figure 6b).
evidence: Supported by dose-response curves from β-galactosidase reporter assays

claim: Pausing of the polymerase at PS1 temporarily decouples the continuous synthesis of the downstream antiterminator sequence, assists in folding of the aptamer domain and allows for sufficient time for the ligand to bind at the structural decision point.
source: Hence, pausing of the polymerase at PS1 temporarily decouples the continuous synthesis of the downstream antiterminator sequence, assists in folding of the aptamer domain and allows for sufficient time for the ligand to bind at the structural decision point.
evidence: Inferred from combination of kinetic data, simulations, and in vivo mutagenesis results

claim: The closure of the PA helix is the last step in accommodation of the ligand in the holo-form of the adenine-sensing riboswitch.
source: Single molecule force extension experiments showed that the structurally similar aptamer domain of the adenine-sensing riboswitch folds co-transcriptional in a hierarchical manner and that the closure of the PA is the last step in accommodation of the ligand in the holo-form (Greenleaf et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenleaf et al., 2008

claim: The formation of the base-paired PA-stem is the committed-step in the off-pathway.
source: These findings and our proposed model are consistent as both conclude that the formation of the base-paired PA-stem is the committed-step in the off-pathway.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with previous single-molecule studies and current kinetic data

claim: One of the two proposed functionally important conformational states of transcriptional riboswitches, the antiterminator state, represents a metastable conformation.
source: For this, we show that one of the two proposed functionally important conformational states of transcriptional riboswitches, the antiterminator state, represents a metastable conformation.
evidence: Supported by structural and kinetic NMR data showing slow refolding from AT to terminator state

claim: Without pausing, the antiterminator conformation is always adopted, independently of ligand concentration.
source: Unexpectedly, our simulations show that without pausing, the antiterminator conformation is always adopted, independently of ligand concentration.
evidence: Supported by kinetic Markov-model simulations

claim: Without pausing, effective regulation could not be achieved by the riboswitch because gene expression could not be turned off.
source: Without pausing, effective regulation could not be achieved by the riboswitch because gene expression could not be turned off.
evidence: Inferred from simulations showing antiterminator always forms without pausing

claim: The polymerases of B. subtilis and E. coli utilize different pausing sequences (e.g. RNA95 and RNA90).
source: In addition we showed that the polymerases of B. subtilis and E. coli utilize different pausing sequences (e.g. RNA95 and RNA90) and therefore differently affect conformational change in the synthesized RNA.
evidence: Supported by transcription assays showing different pause sites for the two polymerases

claim: The effective biotechnological application of transcription-regulating riboswitches in heterologous organisms may require a match between polymerase pausing sequences and the conformational space of the riboswitch.
source: Thus, the effective biotechnological application of transcription-regulating riboswitches in heterologous organisms may require a match between polymerase pausing sequences and the conformational space of the riboswitch.
evidence: Inferred from observation that different polymerases use different pause sites

claim: Riboswitches are cis-regulatory RNA elements controlling cellular processes, in particular transcription and translation.
source: Riboswitches are cis-regulatory RNA elements controlling cellular processes, in particular transcription and translation (Mironov et al., 2002; Nahvi et al., 2002; Mandal et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational riboswitch literature

claim: Riboswitches exert their function via a conformational switch between mutually exclusive base-paired structures induced by binding to a low-molecular weight ligand.
source: They exert their function via a conformational switch between mutually exclusive base-paired structures. This conformational switch is induced by binding to a low-molecular weight ligand (Batey et al., 2004; Noeske et al., 2005; Serganov et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies of riboswitches

claim: The synthesis of RNA is not performed at a constant speed.
source: The synthesis of the RNA is not performed at a constant speed (Maizels, 1973; Darlix and Horaist, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to early transcription studies

claim: Slow conformational changes lead to a variation of the transcription speed of the elongation complex between 2–30 nt/s.
source: Instead, slow conformational changes, from a more competent to a less competent transcription state, lead to a variation of the transcription speed of the elongation complex (EC) between 2–30 nt/s (Davenport et al., 2000; Neuman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies measuring transcription rates

claim: Elemental pausing occurs frequently, but typically lasts only for 1–6 s on average.
source: Thus, transcription rates vary during transcription. This elemental pausing occurs frequently, but typically lasts only for 1–6 s on average, making the overall transcription movement the sum of more and less competent transcription states averaged over the number of RNA polymerases (RNAP) molecules observed.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about transcriptional pausing

claim: At pause-sites, the RNAP speed decreases by a factor of 100 compared to its maximal transcription speed.
source: At pause-sites, the RNAP speed decreases by a factor of 100 compared to its maximal transcription speed (max. 75 nt/s, measured on a specialized DNA template) (Vogel and Jensen, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogel and Jensen, 1994

claim: Pausing can facilitate the folding of certain RNA structures and allow a stabilizing interaction between the nascent RNA and the transcription machinery.
source: Pausing can also facilitate the folding of certain RNA structures and allow a stabilizing interaction between the nascent RNA and the transcription machinery (Pan et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pan et al., 1999

claim: Pausing can be important for effective riboswitch-mediated regulation where co-transcriptional folding is influenced by the transcription speed.
source: Pausing can be important for effective riboswitch-mediated regulation where co-transcriptional folding is influenced by the transcription speed (Wickiser et al., 2005; Perdrizet et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on FMN and B12 riboswitches

claim: The use of a mutant RNA polymerase with deficient pause behavior caused the btuB riboswitch to adopt a non-native structure and to be deficient in ligand binding.
source: The modulation of the available conformational space by altering the transcriptional speed was demonstrated for the btuB riboswitch where the use of a mutant RNA polymerase with deficient pause behavior caused the riboswitch to adopt a non-native structure and to be deficient in ligand binding (Perdrizet et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perdrizet et al., 2012

claim: For the guanine-sensing xpt-pbuX riboswitch from Bacillus subtilis, the conformation of the full-length transcripts is static and exclusively populates the functional off-state.
source: Here, we show that for the guanine-sensing xpt-pbuX riboswitch from Bacillus subtilis, the conformation of the full-length transcripts is static: it exclusively populates the functional off-state but cannot switch to the on-state, regardless of the presence or absence of ligand.
evidence: Supported by NMR data showing only terminator conformation in full-length construct

claim: Only the combined matching of transcription rates and ligand binding enables transcription intermediates to undergo ligand-dependent conformational refolding.
source: We show that only the combined matching of transcription rates and ligand binding enables transcription intermediates to undergo ligand-dependent conformational refolding.
evidence: Supported by combination of kinetic measurements, simulations, and in vivo experiments

claim: GSWPA, GSWPAT, and full-length GSW bind ligand with similar affinities.
source: Both GSW fragments bind the ligand with similar affinities as the full-length riboswitch suggesting formation of the unperturbed aptamer domain (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ITC measurements showing similar Kd values

claim: 59 NMR signals could be detected and resolved in the real-time NMR experiments using selective labeling.
source: Utilizing the above described labeling strategy, we were able to resolve the NMR signals from the ligand, the acceptor domain and the associating or dissociating single RNA strand. In total, 59 signals could be detected, and the reported kinetics have been measured in triplicate experiments and averaged over structural elements in the riboswitch.
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR experimental data

claim: The kinetics reported were measured in triplicate experiments and averaged over structural elements in the riboswitch.
source: In total, 59 signals could be detected, and the reported kinetics have been measured in triplicate experiments and averaged over structural elements in the riboswitch.
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: When ligand binding and annealing of Htrans occur simultaneously, the formation of the terminator conformation is described by two rate constants: k1 = (2 ± 1) × 10−2 s−1 and k2 = (1.2 ± 0.4) × 10−3 s−1.
source: Under the latter conditions, the formation of the terminator conformation was described by two rate constants, k1 = (2 ± 1) 10−2 s−1 reporting on the ligand-induced refolding of the aptamer domain and k2 = (1.2 ± 0.4) 10−3 s−1 characterising the rate-limiting dissociation of helix AT.
evidence: Supported by real-time NMR kinetic measurements

claim: Hypoxanthine was used as the ligand because it is better soluble than guanine.
source: Hypoxanthine was used as the better soluble ligand.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods

claim: The kinetic Markov-model simulations used a transcription rate of 20 nt/s based on the apparent rates determined for B. subtilis polymerase.
source: In order to examine the mutual influence of transcription speed and refolding kinetics on the population of intermediate riboswitch conformations we performed simulations based on a kinetic Markov-model (Prinz et al., 2011) using the experimentally determined refolding and transcription rates of 20 nt/s. This value is based on the apparent rates of transcription determined in the transcription assays for B. subtilis polymerase but taking into account the cellular concentrations of nucleotides, that are approx. 10 times higher than those used in the in vitro transcription reactions (Buckstein et al., 2008) (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on experimental transcription data adjusted for cellular NTP concentrations

claim: Cellular concentrations of nucleotides are approximately 10 times higher than those used in the in vitro transcription reactions.
source: This value is based on the apparent rates of transcription determined in the transcription assays for B. subtilis polymerase but taking into account the cellular concentrations of nucleotides, that are approx. 10 times higher than those used in the in vitro transcription reactions (Buckstein et al., 2008) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buckstein et al., 2008

claim: In the absence of ligand, RNA synthesis is fast enough to allow for formation of the functional on-state apo-form conformation P[AT] both with and without transcriptional pausing.
source: In the absence of ligand, there is no major change as the intermediate conformations occur in a linear succession. In both cases, with and without transcriptional pausing, RNA synthesis is fast enough to allow for formation of the functional on-state apo-form conformation P[AT] (Figure 5b–e).
evidence: Supported by kinetic simulations

claim: Refolding to the thermodynamic most stable functional off-state conformation [PA][TH] in its apo-form only occurs after the polymerase has passed the regulatory point of decision.
source: Refolding to the thermodynamic most stable functional off-state conformation [PA][TH] in its apo-form only occurs after the polymerase has passed the regulatory point of decision.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic simulations showing timing of conformational transitions
